awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: High-Throughput Manufacturing of Ultracompact, High-Contrast Precision Glass Micro-Optics for Next-Generation Photonics and Imaging
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact and commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project lies in making advanced light-based (optical) technologies more affordable and accessible by developing a new way to 3D-print tiny glass parts that control light. These parts, called micro-optics, are used in cameras, lasers, medical tools, communication systems, etc. Currently, making these components is slow, expensive, and requires putting together lots of small pieces. This project introduces a faster and easier method that can create complete light-controlling systems in one step. This could help more people and companies use high-quality optical technology, while also opening new possibilities in fields like telecommunications, healthcare, and self-driving vehicles. The new process costs less, works faster, and allows more creative designs, giving the company a strong advantage in a growing market.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to overcome key limitations in the fabrication of high-performance glass micro-optics by developing a high-throughput 3D printing system utilizing an advanced two-photon polymerization (TPP) technique. Traditional methods for producing glass optics are hindered by high complexity, limited scalability, and elevated costs, and are unable to fabricate monolithic optical systems with integrated functionality. The proposed work will develop a novel 3D printing platform capable of producing high-precision, high-contrast glass micro-optical elements at high throughput. The research objectives include optimizing printing parameters for high optical quality, calibrating TPP printing systems to achieve sub-micron accuracy and uniformity, and fabricating prototype micro-optical systems with integrated optical functions. The project will integrate advances in materials science, ultrafast laser processing, and precision motion control to establish a scalable and alignment-free manufacturing process for micro-optics. The anticipated technical outcome is the demonstration of a reliable fabrication method for complex, compact glass micro-optical systems with superior optical performance, reduced assembly requirements, and improved manufacturability. This research will lay the technical foundation for a disruptive manufacturing approach that enables the widespread adoption of high-performance micro-optics in photonics, medical imaging, and other advanced optical systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
LR InnovOptics Inc. (LRI) developed a system that prints miniature glass optical components using four printing heads simultaneously. Supported by the National Science Foundation’s Small Business Innovation Research Phase I program, the technology integrates optical elements and mechanical supports into a single printed structure. Focused laser light forms three-dimensional shapes in a light-sensitive material, followed by heat treatment to convert the printed structures to glass. This approach addresses limited production capacity, difficult assembly and alignment of miniature micro-optics, and unwanted light passing through their supports.

The four printing heads share a laser source, scanning hardware, and control infrastructure, providing a route to increased production capacity without using four complete systems. Phase I established an operational platform with integrated fabrication software, precision positioning, and optical monitoring. The software connects three-dimensional design preparation with printing control, enabling fabrication of complex optical geometries and systematic evaluation across all four heads.

A principal technical achievement was the integration of local transparency control with glass printing. By adjusting exposure conditions and thermal processing, the team produced transparent optical regions alongside darkened structural features within the same material system. Transparent regions transmit useful light, while darkened regions suppress unwanted light that can reduce image contrast. Repeated experiments across all four printing heads established how laser settings and structure thickness affect light transmission after heat treatment. Process optimization enabled lower laser power and higher scanning speed than originally proposed while maintaining transparency control.

Functional validation included patterned structures that control light transmission and miniature lens systems containing multiple optical elements. Components fabricated by every printhead formed images of a standard resolution target, demonstrating optical functionality across the parallel platform. Miniature lens systems with black lens tubes achieved at least 25% higher image contrast than corresponding systems with transparent tubes. Optimization of thermal treatment also improved image clarity. Fabrication of curved surfaces, fine supporting structures, and complex three-dimensional geometries further demonstrated the platform’s versatility.

The combination of integrated fabrication and transparency control creates opportunities in compact optical imaging, miniature optical sensors, and devices that use light to transmit information. These applications require precise positioning of optical components to form images or guide light between parts of a device. Printing lenses, spacers, and supports as a unified structure could reduce separate component counts and simplify alignment. The work provides a foundation for U.S. manufacturing of customized glass micro-optics and improved access to specialized optical designs for research and product development. Application-specific performance and production reliability will require further qualification.

Phase I also advanced LRI’s commercialization strategy. Through 120 NSF I-Corps customer interviews and subsequent discussions, the team identified demand for both fabrication equipment and finished micro-optical components. Customers sought greater capacity without multiple complete systems, larger printing fields, more clearance for printing tall structures, and automated monitoring with measurements to identify printing failures and dimensional deviations. These findings informed plans for printing systems and materials, catalog products, and custom design and fabrication services for glass and polymer micro-optics.

The company filed 13 provisional patent applications across its broader technology portfolio. Collaborations with research institutions, laboratories, and optical manufacturing organizations supported technical evaluation, technology transfer, and commercialization planning. Phase I established an operating platform, demonstrated functional miniature optics, and identified practical paths to commercialization. These outcomes provide a foundation for U.S. manufacturing of customized glass micro-optics, with potential to simplify the assembly of miniature optical systems and improve access to specialized components for imaging, sensing, and optical communications.
